I'm checking whether `Series._logical_method` casts the result back to bool after aligning the operands as objects, and testing a bool Series `|` with a longer one to see the output dtype and length. I also want to trace whether `DataFrame &=` goes through the same arithmetic path.

I'm tracing the outer alignment in the arithmetic path: the int column turns into float with NaN once the new label is introduced, and the bitwise `&` then fails on float vs int. Next I want to see where `_inplace_method` makes the wrong call, since it aligns with an outer join even though the result is reindexed back to `self` anyway.

I'm weighing whether the fix belongs in `_inplace_method` itself, since it reuses the out-of-place op, which outer-joins and then reindexes back. A left-join alignment of `other` to `self` before the op would keep the int dtype and drop the spurious NaN-induced float upcast.

I'm checking whether the outer-join alignment on the reindexed-back `other` still behaves for nullable Int64 and bool operands. For the bool `|=`, the object-dtype path yields NaN, and I want to confirm whether the result gets cast back to bool before the reindex.

Now I'm looking at the `where` call on the int columns: it inserts NaN for rows the later `loc` filter will drop anyway, which forces the float64 upcast and loses precision on large values. Filtering rows and columns before `where` should keep the integer dtype.

I'm checking the `where` path for the uint64 and bool cases: an all-True mask should leave the integer dtype alone, but mixed differences across rows and columns still force NaN and a float or object result. Series.compare with a boolean mask hits the same upcast.

I'm checking whether `where` behaves the same way: with `keep_equal=True` it's skipped, and when every row differs the mask is all True so it's a no-op. The `keep_shape=True` case has to insert NaN, so a float result there is expected. I also want to confirm that `DataFrame.where` with an all-True condition leaves int64 alone, and then look at how `pivot` builds its result with list `values`.

I'm looking at how `pivot` builds its result with list `values`: taking `DataFrame._values` of mixed int and float columns collapses them into a single float64 array, so the unstack ends up working on one homogeneous block. The harmless cases (a single column, a Series, or the set_index path) keep their own dtypes, so the cleaner fix is to assign the new index onto `data[values]` directly rather than going through `_values`.

Now I'm comparing how `MultiIndex.from_tuples` handles ndarray or Index input against the list path: the array route trims each tuple to the length of the first one, while the list route pads shorter tuples out to the longest length.

I'm checking how `MultiIndex.from_tuples` treats ndarray or Index input. The array route cuts every tuple down to the length of the first one, while the list route pads shorter tuples out to the longest, so I want to see which internal callers hit the array path.

I'm checking the claim that the isin error names the offending length, which would mean isin validates lengths before it reaches from_tuples and behaves correctly. Keys of the right length are fine, and a single too-long tuple given to loc fails with a "Too many indexers" error instead.

I'm checking how `MultiIndex.from_tuples` handles a list of 3-part keys against a 2-level index: the array path takes its width from the first tuple, so the target gets three levels. Then `_recode_for_new_levels` only walks the first two levels and quietly ignores the third, so the keys match on their first two parts alone.

I'm looking at the two cases separately: with mismatched tuple lengths, the array path truncates the keys to the first tuple's width, so the lookup quietly collapses them. With the 3-part keys, the index is built correctly, but `_recode_for_new_levels` only checks the first two levels and ignores the third, so the matching stops early.

I'm working out whether `Index._maybe_downcast_for_indexing` should verify that every tuple matches `self.nlevels` before building a MultiIndex, since that's where the length mismatch could be caught as one root cause. I'm also checking which of the four cases it covers.

I'm weighing whether `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` should only convert to a MultiIndex when every tuple matches `self.nlevels`. Otherwise the mismatched entries would just fail to match and come back as -1, instead of being silently truncated or padded.

I'm settling on the single helper that makes the width decision: `lib.tuples_to_object_array` takes its width from the first tuple, so both `from_tuples` on arrays and `Index.map` inherit that choice. I'll list every routine that reaches it, since that's where the fix would need to hold.

I'm narrowing the root cause to `lib.tuples_to_object_array`, which takes its width from the first tuple, so every caller that routes ndarray or Index input through `from_tuples` inherits that truncation or padding. The three-part keys case is different: the array is built correctly there, but the level-recoding step only checks the first two levels and quietly drops the third.

Checking whether the list path through `ensure_index` produces the same result, since it doesn't use `tupleize_cols` the way the array path does.

I'm weighing whether the four cases share a single root cause or whether the lookup bug is separate from the from_tuples truncation. The three-part key case builds the index correctly, so the failure there sits in the level comparison during get_indexer, not in how the keys are constructed.

I'm mapping the symptoms to their causes: `tuples_to_object_array` explains the truncation and the IndexError, while the three-part key lookups fail in the level comparison instead.

I'm now asking whether the length-3 keys case is a separate failure: the index construction there is correct, so the wrong answer must come from `_extract_level_codes` and `_recode_for_new_levels` comparing only the first levels and ignoring the rest.

I'm settling on `Index._maybe_downcast_for_indexing` as the point where a tuple target gets treated as a MultiIndex, since it only checks the type and whether from_tuples raises, never whether each tuple has `self.nlevels` entries. The comparison then runs through `_recode_for_new_levels`, which only zips the first `self.nlevels` levels and so matches on a prefix. The width itself gets set earlier in `tuples_to_object_array`, which takes it from the first tuple.

I'm going back over the case where the lookup errors trace to two different places, and asking whether a single fix in `tuples_to_object_array` would cover the from_tuples and map symptoms while the lookup symptoms still need their own check.

Checking whether upstream `tuples_to_object_array` also takes its width from the first tuple, and whether `mi.get_indexer` on a 3-level target against a 2-level index gives the same result there.

I'm going back over upstream's `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` and `isin`, to see whether they check tuple length before converting, the same way I'd check the local version.

Checking whether the length-check idea covers the whole picture, or whether the isin validation already added in this checkout is the spot where a matching guard belongs.

I'm settling on `Index._maybe_downcast_for_indexing` as the place where the wrong decision is made: when self is a MultiIndex and the target isn't, it converts the target with `from_tuples` and only backs off on TypeError or ValueError, never checking that each tuple has `self.nlevels` entries. The truncation then comes from the first tuple's width, but nothing downstream checks the key length against the index either.

I'm tracing how the downstream steps trust the width chosen upstream: `_recode_for_new_levels` only walks the index's own level count, and `_wrap_reindex_result` rebuilds the target through `from_tuples`, so the truncated labels end up in the result.

I'm considering `from_tuples` on an object array and `Index.map` as the same kind of failure, since both go through `tuples_to_object_array`, which fixes the width from the first tuple. That makes me wonder whether `MultiIndex.from_tuples` is where the level count is wrongly decided.

I'm weighing a fix at the decision point in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`: only converting the target to a MultiIndex when every key has exactly `self.nlevels` entries, and falling back to a plain object comparison otherwise. That would handle the three lookup cases, though it wouldn't touch the width logic behind `from_tuples` on arrays and `Index.map`, which would still need a separate change to `tuples_to_object_array`.

I'm checking whether fixing `tuples_to_object_array` alone would be enough, and it wouldn't: even with a max-width fix, the lookups on the 2-level keys still come back wrong, and the one-tuple case would match a padded NaN row by mistake. That leaves two separate defects, the ragged-tuple conversion and the missing key-length check on lookup.

I'm checking whether the level-count guard belongs in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`, or in the shared `_extract_level_codes` and `_recode_for_new_levels` helpers that the MultiIndex-to-MultiIndex path also relies on.

I'm narrowing the lookup failures to the level-by-level comparison in `_extract_level_codes` and `_recode_for_new_levels`, which only walks self's level count and never checks the target's length against it.

I'm weighing whether the lookup failures and the truncation are one root cause or two. The truncation comes from taking the width from the first tuple in `tuples_to_object_array`, while the wrong lookup results come from the level-by-level comparison never checking the target's length against `self.nlevels`. Fixing only the first wouldn't resolve the lookups, so I'm leaning toward treating these as two separate defects.

I'm checking whether one check in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing` could stop the wrong conversion, since the keys still need their per-tuple length tested before they become a MultiIndex.

I'm settling on a single fix point in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`: before converting a tuple-valued target into a MultiIndex, check that every key has exactly `self.nlevels` entries, and fall back to plain object comparison if not. That covers the lookup symptoms, but the width bug in `tuples_to_object_array` still needs its own change.

I'm weighing whether the width bug in `tuples_to_object_array` and the missing key-length check on lookup are one defect or two, and it looks like two: the width fix alone doesn't stop the lookups from matching padded keys.

Trying the alternative where `tuples_to_object_array` raises on ragged input, the fallback would catch that and do an object comparison, so the wrong-length keys would come back as -1 instead of matching padded rows. That moves the root cause toward the width logic, though `from_tuples` on a raw ragged array and `Index.map` would still need their own handling.

I'm weighing whether raising on ragged input in `tuples_to_object_array` would route the lookups into the existing fallback, since padding with NaN would still produce a wrong match for the one-tuple case. The uniform three-tuple case would still need its own check.

I'm weighing whether the uniform three-key case, where `[1, 2]` comes back for the reindex, can be explained by the width helper alone, and it can't: that case fails even when every tuple has the same length, which points at the level-count comparison downstream instead.

I'm settling on one root cause here: the level count of each tuple key is never checked against self.nlevels, and the conversion lets the first key decide the width. Because the comparison only walks self's own levels, a mismatched key gets silently truncated or padded instead of being rejected.

I'm settling on one root cause and placing the fix at the decision point in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`, where tuple keys get converted without being checked against the target's level count. The shape decision there goes through `MultiIndex.from_tuples` and `tuples_to_object_array`, which takes the width from the first tuple. I'm also noting that `_recode_for_new_levels` only rejects a target with fewer levels, not one with more.

I'm listing the places that call `MultiIndex.from_tuples` with arrays or Index objects instead of lists. That covers the lookup path in `_maybe_downcast_for_indexing`, `Index.map`, the reindex helpers, and a few union and constructor routines, so each one gets the same width problem from `tuples_to_object_array`.

I'm going through the other places that build a MultiIndex from tuple arrays, checking which of them take the same width-from-first-tuple path. I also want to see whether the in-place operators, `NDFrame.compare`, and `pivot`'s inline `data[values]._values` pattern each repeat the same problem.

I'm going to grep for other places that build the same inline `._values` pattern, then check how the callers of `MultiIndex.from_tuples` get their keys.
